correctness.rationale: For all 0<beta<1 and -1<a<1 the shared-uniform floor coupling has exact expected distance |a||j-k|, giving W1 contraction, unique invariant measure, bounded support and mean beta. The integer inequality j(j-1)>=0 gives the universal variance floor and equality support. Checking the images of 0 and 1 proves both directions of the sharp phase boundary, including equality. Rational balance at beta=1/4 yields the unique three-state law and variance formula; 873 exact checks replayed from verify.py. Model and physical scaling are explicit.

originality.rationale: Targeted published mathematical-results queries, four relevant full-text source inspections, were compared by their mathematical implications. No inspected source contains or entails the stationary minimum-variance iff boundary for a once-rounded uniform-grid affine contraction, nor the exact quarter-grid three-state excess formula. The coupling, elementary integer inequality, and local rounding rule are standard prior tools; equivalent unindexed specializations remain an acknowledged priority risk.
residual_risks: An identical elementary stationary quantized-contraction theorem may appear in older numerical control/dither literature not indexed by target searches.
Wasserstein contraction and two-point minimum variance are classical ingredients; priority attaches only to their exact combined stationary phase classification.
Hardware stochastic rounding with multiple rounded operations, nonuniform grids or finite exponents may behave differently.

value.rationale: The natural engineering question is when stable overrelaxed scalar descent still achieves the information-theoretic stationary quantization floor. The theorem answers it for every target grid phase and all contractive steps, identifies a sharp loss of minimal noise at an explicit point, and computes the first enlarged-support regime without simulation. It separates asymptotic bias, irreducible rounding noise, and support leakage. These facts are not just a restatement of unbiasedness or a generic textbook contraction.
